title: What Is Cache Eviction (LRU)?
sources: Redis docs, 'Key eviction' (redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction): when a cache reaches its maxmemory limit, Redis evicts keys to make room for new data according to maxmemory-policy; allkeys-lru keeps the most recently used keys and removes the least recently used ones; Redis uses an approximated LRU by sampling keys; LFU (least frequently used) is another policy

AWS whitepaper 'Database Caching Strategies Using Redis' - Evictions (docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/database-caching-strategies-using-redis/evictions.html): evictions happen when cache memory is overfilled; LRU is a common eviction policy for most caching use cases

Redis blog 'Cache eviction strategies' (redis.io/blog/cache-eviction-strategies): LRU removes the item that has not been accessed for the longest time, on the idea that recently used data is likely to be used again; cache memory (RAM) is limited and costlier than disk, so caches hold only a subset of data

lines.text: Remember our warm shelf, the cache?
It only has room for three pizzas.
So what happens when a fourth one shows up?
lines.caps: SO WHAT *HAPPENS | WHEN A *FOURTH | ONE SHOWS *UP?

lines.text: Something has to get kicked out,
The most popular rule is LRU,
Every time someone orders a pizza,
it jumps to the front of the line.
The one nobody has touched in the longest time
lines.caps: THE ONE *NOBODY | HAS *TOUCHED | IN THE *LONGEST TIME

lines.text: drifts to the back, and that one gets kicked out.
lines.caps: *DRIFTS | TO THE *BACK | AND *THAT ONE | GETS *KICKED OUT

lines.text: because fast memory is small and pricey.
So popular data stays, and forgotten data goes.
